analysis.one_liner: Requires breast implant makers to pay for surgical removal of implants placed before 1994 and funds safety research.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Commerce Committee in January 1997 and died in a subcommittee when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every breast implant manufacturer to notify anyone who received a silicone or saline implant before 1994 and to pay the full medical costs of surgically removing it, including follow-up surgeries, mammograms, and medication. It would have directed the Health and Human Services Department to research the health effects of silicone and other chemicals used in making implants. It would also have required a signed consent form before any silicone implant surgery, barred doctors from refusing care to implant recipients, and penalized organ and blood organizations that accept donations from implant recipients.
analysis.who_benefits: Women with silicone or saline implants placed before 1994, who could have had them removed — including follow-up care and residual silicone cleanup — at the manufacturer's expense, choosing their own doctor and hospital. Future patients would have gained a standardized informed-consent form detailing health risks, and protection against doctors refusing to treat them because of their implants.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers had to notify implant recipients through national publications and newspapers and pay for removal at the recipient's chosen physician and facility, covering pre- and post-operative care, follow-up surgery to remove residual silicone, scar capsules and granulomas, mammograms, and medication [S3].
The removed implant would remain the property of the woman it came from, to be given to her in appropriate condition [S3].

The Secretary of Health and Human Services would have had to conduct or contract research on the physiological, neurological, and immunological effects of silicone toxicity and other chemicals used in implant manufacturing, including volunteer participants from the multidistrict class action in the Northern District of Alabama [S3].

Physicians could not perform silicone implant surgery without a patient's signed consent form disclosing all known health risks, and could not refuse treatment to a patient simply because she has an implant [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Breast implant manufacturers, who would bear the cost of notifying recipients and paying for removal surgeries for every implant placed before 1994. Implant recipients would also lose the ability to donate organs, since organizations accepting such donations would lose federal grants, and blood banks could lose their license for accepting their blood.

drawbacks.text: The bill would pay for removal of every pre-1994 implant on request, including saline implants, even though removal surgery carries its own risks and is not medically necessary for women without symptoms — an open-ended entitlement that could push many women toward unneeded surgery at manufacturers' expense [S3].
The organ and blood donation provisions would restrict or penalize donations from implant recipients based on unproven health risks, reducing the supply of donated blood and organs [S3].

The removal mandate applied retroactively to implants sold before 1994, raising the prospect of substantial litigation costs for manufacturers and potentially higher prices or withdrawal of implant products from the market [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For women reporting health problems from silicone implants, manufacturer-funded removal and follow-up care plus federally funded toxicity research addressed a real, then-unresolved safety question. But the bill was bluntly drafted: it mandated removal on demand regardless of medical need, including saline implants whose gel-related risks are minimal, and its organ and blood donation bans went well beyond the evidence, cutting donation supply based on unproven contagion-like fears. A narrower version targeting symptomatic patients and funding research alone would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, then to the Health and Environment Subcommittee two weeks later, and no hearing or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, the first day of the 105th Congress [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day [S5].
On January 22, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it sat with no further action [S5].

Twenty-three members cosponsored the bill — 20 Democrats and 3 Republicans — including both progressive members like Charlie Rangel and Barney Frank-era allies and conservative John McCain-adjacent figures such as Henry Hyde [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Breast implant manufacturers were better off: they never faced the removal-payment mandate, and implant recipients got nothing from the federal government.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Implant makers, who faced no mandate

for.name: Rep. James A. Traficant Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Breast Implant Accountability Act on January 7, 1997.

for.name: 20 of 23 cosponsoring House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Rangel, Menendez, Jackson-Lee, Hinchey, Norton, Dellums, and DeLauro.

for.name: 3 of 23 cosponsoring House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Molinari, Hyde, and Thompson.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred on January 7, 1997.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from January 22, 1997, with no action through the end of the Congress.

against.name: Breast implant manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry was defending a wave of implant liability lawsuits in the mid-1990s — Dow Corning filed for bankruptcy in 1995 over implant claims — and a mandatory removal-payment law would have added to that exposure.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were split 20 Democrats and 3 Republicans, with Republicans including Henry Hyde and Susan Molinari among the original backers, but no floor vote ever recorded the chamber's partisan balance.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to notify every pre-1994 recipient and pay the full cost of removal surgery and follow-up care. The bill's death meant they kept no such obligation while courts and settlements handled implant claims privately.

industries.industry: Organ procurement organizations and blood banks
industries.note: They would have lost federal grants or licenses for accepting donations from implant recipients, cutting their supply of donated blood and organs. The provision also stigmatized implant recipients as donors.

The bill would have barred doctors from refusing treatment to implant recipients — a protection for patients — while adding a mandated federal consent form to implant surgery and potentially routing paid removal work to surgeons and hospitals.
